question: All of the following were conclusions of the ETDRS (Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study) EXCEPT:

options.D: aspirin use did not change the risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality
options.C: focal laser increased chance of 2-line gain in visual acuity
options.B: focal laser decreased risk of moderate visual acuity loss
options.A: early scatter photocoagulation resulted in a small reduction in the risk of severe visual loss

explanation: The original ETDRS study addressed 3 main questions: (1) is focal photocoagulation effective for diabetic macular edema? (2) is early scatter photocoagulation effective for earlier stages of diabetic retinopathy? (3) is aspirin effective in delaying progression of diabetic retinopathy? All of the answer choices were conclusions of the ETDRS except that aspirin was actually found to reduce the risk of death and morbidity from cardiovascular causes. explanation: The ETDRS criteria for staging levels of clinically-significant macular edema (CSME) from diabetes only used slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a diagnostic contact lens to detect retinal thickening. Q-A 57-year-old man with proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes presents with sudden vision loss of the left eye after waking up. His vision is 20/30 OD and 20/200 OS. question: Which of the following would be an indication for early vitrectomy?

options.C: Poor vision in the opposite eye
options.B: Extramacular tractional retinal detachment on B-scan ultrasonography

explanation: The patient is presenting with new vitreous hemorrhage in the left eye, most likely due to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). The Diabetic Retinopathy Vitrectomy Study (DRVS) studied the use of vitrectomy in PDR patients. Patients with severe vision loss (5/200 or less) from vitreous hemorrhage and a diagnosis of type 1 DM had better visual outcomes with early vitrectomy versus delayed vitrectomy. However, this advantage was not found in patients with type 2 DM. Therefore, it is reasonable to observe these patients for 4-6 weeks before considering vitrectomy. Other indications for earlier vitrectomy include poor visual acuity in the fellow eye, or ultrasound evidence of a rhegmatogenous detachment or tractional detachment involving the macula. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice "A"). The DRVS also studied early vitrectomy in patients with advanced PDR without vitreous hemorrhage. Patients with severe, active PDR had better visual outcomes with early vitrectomy and vitrectomy was more beneficial with increasing severity of neovascularization. Previous PRP increased the chance of good vision. Patients with complete prior PRP who present with vitreous hemorrhage secondary to PDR can therefore likely be observed for a greater period of time. • (Choice "B"). Patients with dense vitreous hemorrhage obscuring fundus examination should be monitored with B-scan ultrasonography to ensure there is no macula involving tractional detachment or rhegmatogenous detachment that would require prompt intervention. Extramacular tractional retinal detachments can be observed. • (Choice "D"). The DRVS did not show a benefit for early vitrectomy in PDR type II DM patients with severe vitreous hemorrhage. This is visually insignificant as is a "Bergmeister papilla" which is a fibroglial tuft of tissue extending from the optic nerve and which also represents a remnant of the hyaloid system Q-A 64-year-old woman presents for routine examination. She has no visual complaints and best-corrected vision is 20/25 in both eyes. She has no ocular or medical history. Anterior segment examination demonstrates no abnormalities. Fundoscopic examination of the left eye is limited by the finding shown in the photo. The patient’s finding is composed of which of the following?

question: The patient’s finding is composed of which of the following?

options.C: Monoclonal B-cell population with enlarged nuclei and minimal cytoplasm

explanation: The finding shown is asteroid hyalosis, a degenerative disease due to the development of yellow-white disc shaped bodies (“asteroid bodies”) composed of calcium-containing phospholipids within the collagen matrix of the normal vitreous. The cause is unknown, and the majority of patients have unilateral findings. Patients are usually greater than 50-years-old and a link between hypertension and diabetes has been established. Initially, asteroid bodies develop around retinal blood vessels, but may become so extensive that visualization of the fundus is not possible. Despite this, visual acuity is usually only minimally affected. Fluorescein angiography is one imaging modality that can typically bypass the opacities if posterior pathology is suspected and needs to be characterized or monitored. Abnormal vitreoretinal adhesions such as vitreoschisis are well documented in this condition. Even in the presence of a PVD, residual vitreoretinal adhesions are likely and should be expected if patients undergo vitrectomy. Patients rarely require treatment in the form of vitrectomy, however, as they are typically asymptomatic. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice A): Amyloidosis can lead to accumulation of amyloid material in the ocular structures. It is most often seen in primary familial cases of amyloidosis due to a mutation in the transthyretin gene (a dominantly inherited condition); secondary amyloidosis and nonfamilial cases rarely present with ocular findings. Patients with the familial transthyretin gene mutation additionally have a peripheral neuropathy, amyloid nephropathy, and cardiomyopathy. In the eye, the amyloid material is likely excreted from the retinal vasculature with early findings of retinal sheathing, cotton-wool spots, and localized vitreous veils. As the material accumulates, the vitreous is described as a “cob-web” appearance and visual acuity is decreased. Vitrectomy will restore vision and the material removed will demonstrate birefringence with Congo-red staining. • (Choice C): A monoclonal b-cell population with enlarged nuclei would be concerning for primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL). PVRL can be thought of as a subset of primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL). It most often involves the retina, RPE, and vitreous and is frequently of the diffuse large B-cell lymphoma type. When initially presenting in the eye, the disease is a masquerade syndrome that can present with a variety of clinical manifestations and is most frequently misdiagnosed as a posterior uveitis with prominent vitritis. Patients complain of decreased vision and floaters. It is usually a disease of the elderly. PCNSL (disease involving the brain, spinal cord, or meninges) will develop in most patients diagnosed with PVRL, and therefore MRI of the brain is mandatory in any patient with a diagnosis of PVRL. Conversely, 25% of patients with a diagnosis of PCNSL have ocular involvement at time of diagnosis, and approximately 25% of PCNSL patients without initial ocular involvement will develop PVRL. The characteristic lesions of PVRL are sub-RPE sharply defined, yellow- white, tumors (see image). However, the disease can present with many manifestations. For instance, it can simulate a multifocal choroiditis, multiple evanescent white-dot syndrome, an acute retinal necrosis with retinal vasculitis and branch arterial occlusions, optic neuritis, or an isolated vitritis to name a few. Therefore, the diagnosis is difficult. MRI, LP with cytology, and vitrectomy usually all necessary to establish a diagnosis, but can often produce inconclusive results. Treatment involves systemic chemotherapy and/or local therapy with intravitreal methotrexate and rituximab. • (Choice D): Cholesterol-containing crystals describes cholesterolosis, also known as synchysis scintillans, which presents with yellow-white crystalline bodies within the vitreous and anterior chamber. In contrast to asteroid hyalosis, these bodies typically settle inferiorly and are seen in eyes with prior trauma and vitreous hemorrhage. Q-What layer of the retina shown above contains the nuclei of the cells attacked in melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR)?

question: What layer of the retina shown above contains the nuclei of the cells attacked in melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR)?
explanation: MAR is a paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndrome marked by antibody production to retinal bipolar cells in the inner nuclear layer with evidence of bipolar cell dysfunction on electroretinogram (ERG). The classic ERG findings are that of a "negative ERG" with a near normal A-wave but a markedly diminished B-wave. This same pattern of negative ERG is seen with congenital stationary night blindness and retinoschisis. MAR tends to affect predominately rod function while CAR tends to present with both cone and rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) although either can affect rods and/or cones. The vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. OCT is generally normal in MAR. Recently investigators have discovered that at least some cases of MAR are due to antibodies to the TRPM1 cation transduction channel on bipolar cells. In this spectral domain OCT slice, layer A is the inner nuclear layer (where the bipolar cells reside), layer B is the nerve fiber layer, layer C is the ganglion cell layer, and layer D is the outer nuclear layer. mnemonic is MAR (melanoma affects rods) and CAR (Cone and Rods), and the ERG looks like an m (one dip, then flat = no b wave). explanation: This patient has central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR), which is a condition which causes idiopathic serous detachments of the retina. It typically presents between ages 35 and 55 with a 3:1 male-female ratio. Type-A personality, hypertension, Cushing syndrome, sleep apnea, psychopharmacologic medication use, corticosteroid use, and pregnancy are all associated with CSCR. The OCT in this case demonstrates a large amount of subretinal fluid, and fluorescein angiography demonstrates a classic “expansile dot” seen in CSCR . While photodynamic therapy (PDT) can be an effective treatment for CSCR, it does carry the risk of choroidal ischemia (answer D) and subsequent atrophy, which occurs in 4% of eyes. Retinal detachment (answer A), cataract progression (answer B), and optic neuropathy (answer C) are not known complications of PDT. Q-Which of the following medications, taken at high dosages, would be most likely to cause a pigmentary retinopathy leading to vision loss after 6 months of use?

question: Which of the following medications, taken at high dosages, would be most likely to cause a pigmentary retinopathy leading to vision loss after 6 months of use?
explanation: The two main phenothiazines are chlorpromazine (brand: Thorazine) and thioridazine (brand: Mellaril) and have been used as antipsychotic agents especially for the treatment of schizophrenia. Only thioridazine (especially at doses >800 mg/day) has been commonly associated with a severe pigmentary retinopathy that can develop even after only week-to-months of high-dose use. The thioridazine-associated retinopathy classically begins as coarse RPE stippling in the posterior pole. Eventually, patchy atrophy of the RPE and choriocapillaris occurs with a characteristic nummular ("coin-like") pattern. In the late stages, thioridazine retinal toxicty can mimic the appearance of choroideremia or Bietti crystalline dystrophy. Visual dysfunction including blurred vision, visual field loss, and night blindness is common and can still progress even if the medication is stopped. In contrast, pigmentary retinopathy is rare with chlorpromazine use. Common ocular side effects of chlorpromazine use includes: pigmentation of the eyelids, interpalpebral conjunctiva, cornea, and anterior lens capsule; as well as anterior and posterior subcapsular cataracts. Hydroxychloroquine toxicity is relatively rare especially with less than 5 years of use. It begins with a subtle granular depigmentation of the paracentral RPE. Eventually, continued exposure to hydroxychloroquine can lead to bilateral atrophic bull's eye maculopathy with paracentral scotomas. In severe cases, it can cause widespread retinal atrophy with severe visual loss. Typical screening tests for hydroxychloroquine toxicity include 10-2 static perimetry (for non-Asians), 24-2 or 30-2 static perimetry (for Asians), and SD-OCT. The earliest finding on OCT is disruption of the parafoveal ellipsoid zone. Q-Which of the following diseases is the leading cause of blindness in the United States for patients aged 20-64 years?

I think most authorities would agree that cataract is the #1 cause of worldwide blindness, while the other causes are debatable) Q-When a patient is taking hydroxychloroquine, which of the following oral medications has a synergistic retinal toxicity?

question: When a patient is taking hydroxychloroquine, which of the following oral medications has a synergistic retinal toxicity?
explanation: Concomitant use of hydroxychloroquine and tamoxifen can have a five- fold increased risk of retinal toxicity. This is relevant because tamoxifen is often taken as adjuvant therapy for years after a person has had breast cancer. Given that hydroxychloroquine is also a chronic medication, it is likely that their paths will cross in a few of your patients. Vision loss may progress even after cessation of the medication. Other relevant facts about hydroxychloroquine and screening for retinal toxicity are that the highest recommended dose is 5 mg/kg/day of total body weight. The recommendations changed from dosing based on ideal body weight to total body weight. This was done to avoid overdosing in obese (due to physician error in not accounting for ideal body weight) and very thin patients (who would have their dose increased because their weight is actually below ideal body weight). Hydroxychloroquine is also cleared by the kidneys so patients with low GFRs may be at risk of retinal toxicity. The revised screening recommendations also include objective tests such as spectral domain OCT, multifocal ERG, and fundus autofluorescence. Asian patients may show an extramacular pattern of retinal damage and thus screening with 24-2 static perimetry may benefit this population. Q-According to the 2016 AAO (American Academy of Ophthalmology) Update, which of the following tests constitute accepted screening for retinal toxicity from hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine?

question: According to the 2016 AAO (American Academy of Ophthalmology) Update, which of the following tests constitute accepted screening for retinal toxicity from hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine?

options.D: 10-2 visual field in non-Asian patients, spectral domain OCT, fundus autofluorescence
options.C: 10-2 visual field in Asian patients, spectral domain OCT, multifocal ERG
options.B: 24-2 visual field in non-Asian patients, Amsler grid, spectral domain OCT
options.A: 10-2 visual field in non-Asian patients, fundus autofluorescence, full-field ERG

explanation: The AAO's 2016 Update on "Recommendations on Screening for Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy" recommends getting automated visual fields and spectral-domain OCT for routine primary screening given their wide availability. Specifically, the update recommends: • 10-2 SITA for non-Asian patients • 24-2 or 30-2 SITA for Asian patients. The rationale for this is that toxicity often manifests beyond the macula in this patient demographic. Other helpful screening tests: • Multifocal ERG • Autofluorescence (AF). Increased autofluorescence in parafoveal / extramacular areas may precede areas of thinning on SD-OCT. Late RPE loss appears as an area of reduced AF. Tests not recommended for screening: • Fundus exam and photography. Obviously, if changes are visible on ophthalmoscopy (e.g. Bull's eye maculopathy), then the damage is already very advanced and would have been detected by the other methods much earlier. • Time-domain OCT. • Fluorescein angiography. This test will detect RPE defects, but these are considered late changes. • Full-field ERG. • Amsler grid. • Color vision testing. • Electro-oculogram (EOG). Other clinical pearls from this update include: • The most frequent region of the retina to show early damage is inferotemporal which corresponds with a superonasal field defect. • SD-OCT shows localized thinning of the photoreceptor layers in the parafoveal region in non-Asian eyes or near the arcades in Asian eyes. explanation: The retinal lesions, associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) resemble those of congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE). However, the lesions in FAP can be distinguished from CHRPE by the following characteristics: • Smaller. • More ovoid. • More irregular and often with a "fish tail" configuration. • Less uniform in pigmentation. • Multiple. • Bilateral. The presence of >4 widely-spaced, small lesions which are bilateral are suggestive of FAP. This condition is caused by mutations of the adenomatous polyposis (APC) gene and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with incomplete penetrance. CHRPE are usually uniformly heavily-pigmented except for occasional depigmented lacunae. Patients with probable FAP should undergo a screening colonoscopy to look for suspicious colonic polyps. options.C: cerebellar hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma
options.B: spinal cord tumors and liver cysts

explanation: The photograph depicts a redidsh-orange vascular tumor that is fed by a dilated, tortuous retinal artery and drained by an engorged vein. These features are classic for a retinal capillary hemangioblastoma. These tumors can occur in both hereditary (autosomal dominant) and sporadic forms. When there are only hemangioblastomas of the eye, the condition is called von Hippel lesions, but when there is also central nervous system and visceral involvement, it is called von Hippel- Lindau syndrome. Vision loss from these lesions can occur from serous retinal detachment or exudate collecting underneath the macula. Vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment are other causes of vision loss in von Hippel-Lindau disease. Other key facts regarding VHL syndrome: • Caused by mutation of a gene (VHL - a tumor suppressor gene) on chromosome 3p26. • Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern; high penetrance (varies by mutation) and variable expression. • Central nervous system tumors can include: 20% of VHL patients have hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum, medulla, pons, and spinal cord. • Other findings include: renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytomas, cysts of the kidney/pancreas/liver, cardiac rhabdomyomas. All of the answer choices are possible systemic manifestations of von Hippel-Lindau disease. The primary cause of death from this condition is from cerebellar hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma. Therefore, when this characteristic capillary hemangioma is found, a thorough systemic evaluation should be undertaken. question: A 45-year-old woman has been newly-diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. The patient weighs 60 kilograms. Her rheumatologist wishes to start her on hydroxychloroquine for the patient's joint aches. The patient's ocular exam is unremarkable. Which of the following is the maximal dose this patient could take on a daily basis?
explanation: The most recent recommendations from the American Academy of Ophthalmology state that all patients should keep daily hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) use to ≤ 5.0 mg/kg of real body weight. Thus, the maximum allowed dosage for this patient would be 5 * 60 = 300 mg/day. For patients taking ≤ 5.0 mg/kg/day, the estimated risk of HCQ retinal toxicity is <1% during the first 5 years of treatment and <2% up to 10 years. However, the risk increases to ~20% after 20 years of treatment. The most important risk factors for HCQ retinal toxicity are: • Daily dose >5.0 mg/kg of real body weight. • Duration of use >5 years • Renal disease. HCQ and chloroquine are both cleared to a significant degree by the kidneys. Thus, renal function needs to be monitored closely to prevent unusually high serum levels of these medications. • Tamoxifen use. The risk of HCQ toxicity is increased ~5x with the concomitant use of this breast cancer drug. The mechanism underlying this increased risk is not understood. • Macular disease. Significant central photoreceptor loss could interfere with the tests (e.g. 10-2, SD-OCT) used to screen for HCQ retinal toxicity. Q-A 44-year-old man presents for an annual eye exam. question: Which of the following medications is responsible for her fundus findings?
explanation: Interferon alpha-2a (IFA2a) is a historical treatment for viral hepatitis and has been associated with the development of an occlusive retinal microvasculopathy characterized by multiple cotton-wool spots, retinal hemorrhages, and areas of capillary nonperfusion on fluorescein angiography. Patients are usually minimally symptomatic but may experience paracentral visual field defects. Diabetes and hypertension are associated with a higher risk of development of retinopathy from IFA2a use. The fundus findings are typically reversible on cessation of the drug. WRONG ANSWERS: • Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is an agent used mainly for the treatment of lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. Development of HCQ maculopathy is dependent on the dose and duration of use. The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) recommends a maximum of dose of 5.0 mg/kg real weight. Toxicity involves the degeneration of the RPE and overlying sensory retina initially in an enlarging ring around the macula in a bull’s eye pattern that can later involve the fovea. The earliest sign of toxicity is paracentral visual field loss. After five years of use, the AAO recommends screening patients annually with at least visual field testing and OCT. • Nicotinic acid can be used for the treatment of hyperlipidemia and can rarely cause cystoid macula edema (CME) in patients receiving high doses (1.5-5g/day). The CME in this condition interestingly is not visible on fluorescein angiography. explanation: The Standard Care vs. Corticosteroid for Retinal Vein Occlusion (SCORE) Study CRVO was a multicenter, randomized, clinical trial of 271 participants that compared the efficacy and safety of 1-mg and 4-mg doses of preservative-free intravitreal triamcinolone with observation for eyes with vision loss associated with macular edema secondary to a perfused central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). After one year, 27 percent of patients in the 1 milligram group and 26 percent of patients in the 4 milligram group experienced a visual gain of three or more lines. Only 7 percent of patients in the observation group experienced a similar visual gain. Patients in the corticosteroid treatment groups were five times more likely to have a substantial visual gain at one year. These results appeared to last up to two years, though the two-year results included a smaller number of patients. Participants who received the 4 milligram dose had the highest rates of cataract formation, cataract surgery, and elevated pressure within the eye, indicating that the 1 milligram dose is safer for patients. This study established intravitreal triamcinolone as an improvement over the previous standard of care observation in the treatment of CRVO-associated macular edema. explanation: The Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion Study (BVOS) demonstrated that grid laser was helpful in increasing the chances of 20/40 vision and a gain in >= 2 lines of vision for patients with chronic (>3 months) macular edema caused by a BRVO. However, this benefit was only seen in patients with intact macular perfusion. In cases of macular non-perfusion, no treatment is indicated. Some key findings of the BVOS: • For BRVO with macular edema, there was spontaenous improvement in ~1/3 of patients after 3 months. • Again, for patients with BRVO with macular edema for >3 months and 20/40 or worse vision, the chances of gaining 2 lines of vision doubled by performing grid laser. • Forty (40) percent of treated eyes had worse than 20/40 and 12% of treated eyes had 20/200 or worse vision after 3 years. These statistics demonstrated that laser treatment of BRVO patients oftentimes did not result in good visual outcomes. • For eyes without neovascularization (NV), eyes treated with sectoral PRP developed significantly less NV than non-treated eyes. • For eyes with NV, eyes treated with sectoral PRP developed significantly less vitreous hemorrhage. This report from the BVOS recommended only performing sectoral PRP after NV developed. Of course, with the advent of anti-VEGF agents, the treatment recommendations of the BVOS are now outdated. explanation: The lesion is a retinal cavernous hemangioma. These tumors are hamartomas composed of clusters of thin-walled saccular aneurysms filled with stagnate venous blood and give the appearance of a “cluster of grapes”. They can present within the retina or the optic nerve head. Overlying the lesion, there may be variable amounts of fibrous membranes that can occasionally be associated with vitreous traction and preretinal, or vitreous hemorrhage. The surrounding retinal blood vessels are normal and fluorescein angiography demonstrates delayed filling of the lesion with layering within the saccular aneurysms in the late frame as demonstrated in the photo. Leakage is not seen. Complications such as exudation and hemorrhage are rare. Typically, these lesions are asymptomatic, but can cause loss of vision if present in the macula or if vitreous traction causes vitreous hemorrhage. These tumors do not increase in size and treatment with photocoagulation or cryotherapy to obliterate the tumor is rarely required. Retinal cavernous hemangiomas are usually solitary, sporadic, and unassociated with any systemic condition. There is evidence, however, that some cases can be inherited as an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome associated with cerebral, optic pathway, brainstem, and skin cavernous malformations which typically present with neurological manifestations before the age of 25. As such, neuroimaging and a thorough skin examination should be obtained in any patient with a retinal cavernous hemangioma. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice A): Retinal capillary hemangiomas (also known as retinal angiomas, or retinal capillary hemangioblastomas) are congenital, hereditary capillary hamartomas of the retina and optic nerve head. Retinal tumors present as red or pink lesions that are usually associated with arteriovenous (AV) shunting between a dilated tortuous feeding artery and large draining vein. Optic nerve tumors are often flat, not associated with AV shunting, and may be confused for papilledema or a peripapillary choroidal neovascular membrane. Leakage and exudation from these tumors will cause decreased vision. Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity and is characterized by retinal and CNS angiomas as well as kidney, liver, pancreas, and epididymis angiomas, cysts or adenomas. Other systemic tumors include renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytomas. The diagnosis of a retinal capillary hemangioma requires a systemic workup with genetic testing. Cerebral angiomas and renal cell carcinomas are the leading cause of death in these patients. • (Choice B): Although the majority of retinal cavernous hemangiomas are sporadic, some are associated with a likely autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome with cerebral, optic pathway, brainstem, and skin cavernous malformations. Cerebral hemangiomas can lead to seizures, intracranial hemorrhage, and death. Therefore, neuroimaging should be obtained to rule out this possibility. • (Choice D): Ocular toxocariasis is an inflammatory condition in response to parasitic antigens left by a dead or dying parasite Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati. explanation: This patient presents with an acute branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO), bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and encephalopathy. These findings constitute the clinical triad of Susac syndrome. Susac syndrome is a rare disorder with a female to male predilection of 3 to 1. The typical age at diagnosis is in young adults 20-40 years old. As of present, the exact cause of Susac syndrome is not known, but it is hypothesized to be an immune- mediated injury involving the endothelium of the retina, cochlea and cerebral vasculature. The BRAO that occurs in Susac syndrome can occur at any time during the course of the disease. Its negative effect on vision varies since it can affect just small, peripheral retinal areas, or much larger areas of the macula. Yellowish-white retinal wall "Gass plaques" can be found in this disease and are often found at sites other than arteriolar bifurcations (unlike Hollenhorst plaques). The hearing loss in this disease is typically bilateral, asymmetric, and sensorineural. It also can vary from mild/insidious to severe/acute. Unfortunately, this hearing loss is typically permanent. The encephalopathy in Susac syndrome can manifest with headache (often confused with migraine), confusion, memory problems, ataxia, and personality changes. As of present, there is no standard treatment regimen for Susac syndrome. However, most experts start with intravenous methylprednisolone. Other alternative and adjunctive treatments include: intravenous immunoglobulin (*after* 1 month of oral prednisone), cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, plasmapheresis, infliximab, and etanercept. options.A: Reduced blood flow from carotid artery obstruction

explanation: The patient is presenting with a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The most common cause of a CRAO is embolic, although vascular narrowing, thrombosis, arterial spasm, and reduced blood flow via carotid/ophthalmic artery obstruction, decreased systemic blood pressure, or elevated intraocular pressure can all lead to occlusive retinal arterial disease. The most common etiology of emboli is from ulcerated atheromatous plaques of the carotid artery, followed by cardiac valvular disease. Patients with an embolic CRAO typically experience sudden, painless vision loss that may be preceded by episodes of amaurosis fugax. Ocular manifestations include widespread ischemic whitening of the inner retina most prominent in the posterior pole with sparing of the fovea (“cherry-red spot”). The narrowest part of the central retinal artery is where it perforates the dural sheath of the optic nerve and emboli here will not be visualized on ophthalmic examination. Three major types of emboli occur: 1. Platelet-fibrin: gray-white, elongated plaques associated with large-vessel arteriosclerosis. 2. Cholesterol (Hollenhorst): yellow globules associated with carotid artery disease. 3. Calcific: solid, white plaques associated with cardiac valvular disease Both platelet-fibrin and cholesterol emboli are soft and become fragmented easily. Additionally, during an acute obstruction, collateral flow can develop. As such, fluorescein angiography (FA) will rarely show complete absence of arterial flow. Rather, it will demonstrate a significant flow reduction which will continue to be depressed even after obstruction is relieved due to collapse of the capillary bed by an ischemic and swollen inner retina. Typically, the retinal whitening resolves several weeks following the event, but flow usually is still reduced likely due to loss of the capillary bed in the remaining necrotic inner retina. Visual prognosis is dependent on the duration of obstruction but is generally poor. There is no proven treatment for CRAO, and patients should emergently be worked up for sources of emboli with evaluation of the carotids and heart for secondary prevention of future embolic events. In patients in which giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a concern, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein should be measured. WRONG ANSWERS: A-C: The most common cause of a CRAO is embolic, although vascular narrowing, thrombosis, arterial spasm, and reduced blood flow via carotid/ophthalmic artery obstruction, decreased systemic blood pressure, or elevated intraocular pressure can all lead to occlusive retinal arterial disease. explanation: The late phase angiogram shows the classic petalloid pattern of fluorescein leakage consistent with cystoid macular edema (CME). The OCT findings, which show cystic areas of low reflectivity, are classic for the diagnosis. CME is caused by abnormal perifoveal retinal capillary permeability and can occur in many conditions such as: • post-intraocular surgery (e.g. cataract surgery; where it is called Irvine- Gass syndrome) • diabetic retinpathy • branch or central retinal vein occlusion • any type of uveitis (especially pars planitis) • panretinal photocoagulation • retinitis pigmentosa • subretinal disease processes (e.g. choroidal neovascularization) • niacin supplementation Post-cataract surgery CME typically occurs 6-10 weeks postoperatively. In uncomplicated cataract surgery, there is a high rate of spontaneous resolution over the course of 6 months, but most clinicians will treat to hasten its resolution especially if the patient is symptomatic. Typical management starts with topical corticosteroids and NSAIDs (e.g. bromfenac). If the CME is unresponsive to topical treatment, then periocular (e.g. subTenon Kenalog®) or intravitreal (e.g. Triesence®) injection of steroid preparations are commonly employed. Intravitreal (not subconjunctival) anti-VEGF agents (e.g. ranibizumab) are occasionally employed for the treatment for pseudophakic CME. Subconjunctival and topical anti-VEGF agents (e.g. bevacizumab) are occasionally used to induce regression of corneal neovascularization in the setting of high-risk corneal grafts. If the cataract surgery was complicated by vitreous loss or iris prolapse, then these anatomical issues are addressed. For example, a YAG vitreolysis can be performed to break apart any vitreous strands adherent to the cornea (i.e. causing traction). If there is iris incarcerated in the wound, this tissue can be reposited back into the eye to resolve any persistent inflammation that could be contributing to chronic CME. explanation: This is a classic example of a relatively newly described diagnosis, paracentral acute middle maculopathy (PAMM) which most experts believe to be a variant of acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN). Both are thought to be caused by retinal ischemia although AMN typically involves the deeper portions of the retina (e.g. the ellipsoid region) while the aptly named PAMM results in middle retinal lesions caused by ischemia of the deep retinal capillary bed just deep to the inner nuclear layer. AMN is an exceedingly rare disease initially described in 1975. This disease tends to affect females (approximately 85%) in their reproductive years (mean age 27). The etiology remains unknown but reports are published of associated oral contraceptive use, preceding viral illness, and recent use of stimulants such as epinephrine or ephedrine. Both AMN and PAMM are clinical diagnoses marked by the presence of one or more reddish-brown central macular round or “wedge shaped” lesions that correlate precisely to the location of the patients’ paracentral relative scotomas. Spectral domain OCT (SD-OCT) and infrared (IR) fundus photographs help immensely with diagnosis of both AMN and PAMM. You can see in this example that the lesions exhibited on SD-OCT and IR imaging (used for fundus visualization during OCT image capture) are not clearly seen on the fundus exam nor on fundus autofluorescence images. explanation: The Standard Care vs. Corticosteroid for Retinal Vein Occlusion (SCORE) Study evaluated both central retinal vein occlusions and branch retinal vein occlusions. SCORE CRVO was a multicenter, randomized, clinical trial of 271 participants that compared the efficacy and safety of 1-mg and 4-mg doses of preservative- free intravitreal triamcinolone with observation for eyes with vision loss associated with macular edema secondary to a perfused central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). After one year, 27 percent of patients in the 1 milligram group and 26 percent of patients in the 4 milligram group experienced a visual gain of three or more lines. Only 7 percent of patients in the observation group experienced a similar visual gain. Patients in the corticosteroid treatment groups were five times more likely to have a substantial visual gain at one year. These results appeared to last up to two years, though the two-year results included a smaller number of patients. Participants who received the 4 milligram dose had the highest rates of cataract formation, cataract surgery, and elevated pressure within the eye, indicating that the 1 milligram dose is safer for patients. This study established intravitreal triamcinolone as an improvement over the previous standard of care observation in the treatment of CRVO-associated macular edema. SCORE BRVO was a multicenter, randomized clinical trial of 411 participants that compared the efficacy and safety of 1-mg and 4-mg doses of preservative-free intravitreal triamcinolone with standard care (grid photocoagulation in eyes without dense macular hemorrhage and deferral of photocoagulation until hemorrhage clears in eyes with dense macular hemorrhage) for eyes with vision loss associated with macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO). After one year, 29 percent of patients in the laser treatment group, 26 percent of patients in the 1 milligram corticosteroid injection group, and 27 percent of patients in the 4 milligram injection group experienced a visual gain of three or more lines. These results appeared to last up to three years, though the three-year results included a smaller number of patients. However, patients who received either dose of corticosteroid medication were more likely to develop a cataract or experience elevated pressure within the eye than patients who received laser treatment. Also, between one and two years after enrollment in the study, patients in the 4 milligram group underwent more cataract surgeries than patients in the other groups. The researchers recommended that grid photocoagulation remain the standard of care and the benchmark against which other treatments are compared in future clinical trials. explanation: The fundus photograph shows the diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages that are typical for a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). There are two main subtypes of CRVO: non-ischemic and ischemic. The ischemic form is defined by at least 10 disc areas of capillary non-perfusion on fluorescein angiography (posterior pole view). The CVOS (Central Retinal Vein Occlusion Study) found that prophylatic PRP for ischemic CRVO did *not* completely prevent the development of iris or angle neovascularization and that future PRP was less effective. Specifically, 20% with ischemic CRVO still developed iris/angle neovascularization. Therefore, PRP is only recommended when iris or angle neovascularization first occurs. The CVOS also found that macular grid laser did *not* significantly improve visual acuity in CVO patients with macular edema. However, there was a trend toward improved outcomes for younger (<65 years old) patients, with *non-ischemic CRVO*, who received macular grid laser. Therefore, many retinal specialists will consider macular grid laser for these younger, perfused patients. Editor's note: of course with the results of the BRAVO/CRUISE studies, use of anti-VEGF medications like ranibizumab is now the most popular way of treating macular edema associated with branch and central vein occlusions. For macular edema caused by a BRVO, the BVOS (Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion Study) recommended waiting for 3 months to allow for spontaneous resolution of edema and blood. Eyes with macular edema are then treated with grid laser if visual acuity is 20/40 or worse. In addition, a fluorescein angiogram (FA) must demonstrate the absence of macular non-perfusion. If macular non-perfusion is present on FA, then laser should not be undertaken. explanation: This patient presents with the typical "blood and thunder" fundus appearance of a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). This is demonstrated by the diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages, swollen optic nerve, and acutely-decreased vision. The CRUISE study1, published in 2010, investigated the effect of intravitreal ranibizumab (0.3 and 0.5 mg doses) versus sham injection on CRVO-associated macular edema involving the fovea. The treatment protocol consisted of monthly intravitreal ranibizumab injections for 6 months followed by a 6-month "observation period" during which all participants could receive additional injections according to a pre-specified reinjection protocol. This pivotal study showed that both ranibizumab dosages were highly effective in improving the vision of patients with CRVO-associated macular edema. Specifically, at the initial 6-month endpoint, the mean change from baseline visual acuity (the primary endpoint) was a gain of 12.7 and 14.9 letters in the ranibizumab groups compared to only 0.8 letters in the sham injection group. The drug groups also showed significant positive results for other visual parameters (e.g. gain of at least 15 letters) as well as quality-of-life scores. The same issue of Ophthalmology in which the CRUISE study was published also contained articles for the initial BRAVO2 and Ozurdex3 results. Briefly, the BRAVO trial was an analogous trial to CRUISE which enrolled patients with BRVO-associated macular edema. It showed similar results to the CRUISE trial. The Ozurdex trial (GENEVA) (Answer "B") showed the efficacy of a single dexamethasone intravitreal implant on macular edema associated with either BRVOs or CRVOs. explanation: Leber miliary aneurysms (i.e. unilateral parafoveal telangiectasia type 1) typically occurs in males and resembles a macular variant of Coats disease with a circinate type of exudates. When edema is present, laser photocoagulation may be indicated and can be successful in resolving exudation. Type 2 bilateral parafoveal telangiectasia has equal sex predilection and affects both eyes. Perifoveal (mostly temporal) retinal changes typically include thickening, loss of transparency with grayish appearance, small telangiectatic vessels, and a cystic appearance of the fovea. Choroidal neovascularization may develop. Approximately one-third of patients with this variant will have an abnormal glucose tolerance test. This condition does not typically respond to laser photocoagulation but may show some improvement with anti-VEGF agents. Patients with type 3 bilateral parafoveal telangiectasia with retinal capillary obliteration show vision loss from the loss of perifoveal capillaries. Type 3, like type 2, does not respond well to laser photocoagulation. Retinal macroaneurysms are acquired ectasias of mostly second-order retinal arterioles. Vision loss may occur from occlusion of the arteriole or due to hemorrhage. Hemorrhage may span all layers of the retina (e.g. vitreous hemorrhage, sub-ILM, intraretinal or subretinal). Retinal edema is also a cause of vision loss in these cases. The most common association with retinal arterial macroaneurysms is chronic hypertension (two-thirds of cases). Laser photocoagulation can be considered in cases of vision loss due to macular edema. Thrombosis and subsequent arterial obstruction is a possible complication of laser photocoagulation treatment of macroaneurysms. explanation: The patient has an acquired retinal macroaneurysm (RAM) located on the inferior arcade. RAM develop in the sixth to seventh decade of life, typically off of a third order arterial branch. The most common risk factor is hypertension. They are more common in women, and are more frequent in the right eye, but are bilateral in 10% of cases. Visual symptoms are typically due to exudation spreading into the macula. However, spontaneous bleeding may also occur (sometimes precipitated by Valsalva); are at multiple retinal levels (e.g., subretinal, under the internal limiting membrane, subhyaloid, and vitreous); and cause sudden vision loss. Pathology shows a break in the arterial wall closed off by a fibrin platelet clot and surrounded by varying amounts of blood, exudate, macrophages, hemosiderin, and a fibroglial reaction. Prognosis is excellent with many aneurysms spontaneously closing by thrombosis after a period of exudation or bleeding. Patients with chronic exudation or bleeding in the macula are at greatest risk of permanent vision loss. As spontaneous healing is frequent, treatment is not often indicated, but should be considered with persistent exudation within the fovea. Treatment is with laser photocoagulation with large- spot-size and long-duration focused at the aneurysm. WRONG ANSWERS: • Spontaneous rupture can cause acute loss of vision; however most bleeding RAMs have an excellent prognosis with spontaneous resolution. • Multiple lesions may develop due to focal arterial wall aging defects, but this is not an indication for treatment. • Hemorrhage may occur at multiple levels of the retina (e.g., subretinal, under the internal limiting membrane, subhyaloid, and vitreous). However, most bleeding RAMs have an excellent prognosis with spontaneous resolution. This patient would benefit from AREDS vitamin supplementation to reduce the chance of developing advanced AMD. The original AREDS vitamin formulation consisted of vitamin C, vitamin E, beta carotene, zinc oxide, and cupric oxide. Caution should be used in using beta-carotene in current or past smokers since there appears to be a higher risk of lung cancer for this sub-population of patients. The more recent AREDS2 formulation replaces the beta-carotene component with lutein and zeaxanthin. A post-hoc subgroup analysis done in AREDS2 compared lutein + zeaxanthin + AREDS without beta carotene versus the original AREDS formulation (i.e. had beta-carotene). This analysis found a hazard ratio of 0.82 in favor of the lutein + zeathanin + AREDS without beta carotene for progression to advanced AMD. Thus, the AREDS2 recommended that the beta-carotene component be completely replaced with lutein + zeathanin (in addition to the concern of increased lung cancer in former/current smokers). This was the control group in the AREDS study. Actually, 0.45% of these patients progressed to advanced AMD. • Category 2 (Early AMD) -- extensive small drusen, pigment abnormalities, or at least 1 intermediate (63-124 microns) size druse. These patients had only a 1.3% probability of progression to advanced AMD by 5 years. • Category 3 (Intermediate AMD) -- extensive intermediate drusen; at least one large ( ≥125 microns) druse; or noncentral geographic atrophy (GA). These patients had a 18% probability of progression to advanced AMD by 5 years. • Category 4 (Advanced AMD) -- at least one of the following: o GA involving the foveal center o presence of CNV o serous or hemorrhagic detachment of the neurosensory retina or RPE o Retinal hard exudates o Subretinal and sub-RPE fibrovascular proliferation o Disciform scar o (Thus, if a patient had advanced AMD in one eye, then the AREDS found a 43% probability of progression to advanced AMD in the fellow eye at 5 years) Since these categories are somewhat difficult to remember, a simplified 4-point grading system was developed by AREDS to classify the severity of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to predict an individual's risk of developing advanced AMD in one eye. This grading system is as follows: • presence of any pigment abnormalities -- 1 point • presence of 1 or more large (≥125 micron in diameter) drusen -- 1 point • presence of neovascular AMD -- 2 points • for patients with no large drusen, presence of bilateral intermediate (63- 124 microns) drusen -- 1 point These risk factors are added over both eyes and have a range from 0 to 4. explanation: The BCSC specifically mentions two specific susceptibility genes for the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD): • CFH (1q31) o This gene codes for complement factor H. o The CFH Y402H mutation confers a 4.6-fold increased risk for AMD when heterozygous and a 7.4-fold increased risk when homozygous. • ARMS2 (10q26) o "Age-Related Maculopathy Susceptibility 2" o Poorly understood gene product and function o ARMS2 A69S mutation confers a 2.7-fold increased risk for AMD when heterozygous and an 8.2-fold increased risk when homozyous. If an individual is homozygous for these mutations in both genes, the risk for AMD is an astonishing 50-fold higher. Mutations in CHM are responsible for choroideremia. This is an X-linked recessive disease which is characterized by widespread and progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris. Studies have localized the CHM gene product to the RPE. These individuals typically develop night blindness during the first or second decade of life, and later develop ring scotomata similar to retinitis pigmentosa. However, most patients with this disease maintain good central visual acuity for 4 or 5 decades. Mutations in VMD2 (BEST1; chromosome 11) are responsible for Best disease. These individuals typically have a yellow, "yolk-like" macular lesion present in childhood. This "yolk" eventually breaks down leaving a mottled geographic atrophy pattern. Individuals with Best disease have relatively-good (e.g. 20/30) vision despite the dramatic appearance of the macular lesions. This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Mutations in OAT are responsible for gyrate atrophy. This condition is characterized by geographic paving-stone-like areas of atrophy that coalesce to form a scalloped border between abnormal and normal RPE. Gyrate atrophy is an autosomal recessive condition. Mutations in OAT result in markedly-high elevations of ornithinewhich is toxic to the retina and choroid. Treatment consists of dietary arginine restriction (if possible) and vitamin B6 supplementation (if the patient is actually responsive to this therapy). Other findings in gyrate atrophy include: posterior subcapsular cataracts, and high myopia with high astigmatism. Visual acuity is usually normal in these patients until the age of 10 years.
